title: Camillus and the Treacherous Schoolmaster
text:
In 394 BC, according to Roman tradition, the general Marcus Furius Camillus was besieging Falerii, a town of the Faliscans north of Rome. The siege was dragging on, and the town was well defended.

Livy and Plutarch tell the story. The Faliscans entrusted the education of the children of their leading families to a schoolmaster, who took them out of the town each day for walks and exercise. In the time of war he kept doing so, taking them a little farther each day. One day he led them all the way into the Roman camp, brought them before Camillus, and offered them as hostages: with these children in Roman hands, he said, the town would have to surrender.

Camillus refused. Plutarch has him say that even in war good men observe certain laws, and that a great general should rely on his own virtue and not on other men's vices. He ordered the schoolmaster stripped and his hands bound behind his back, gave the boys rods, and told them to drive their teacher back to the town, whipping him as they went.

The Faliscans, who had been in despair over the loss of their children, saw them return, whipping the traitor. Moved by the Roman general's honesty, the town decided that it would rather trust Rome's justice than keep fighting. They sent envoys and surrendered to Camillus on terms.
lesson: Refusing an unfair advantage can win more than taking it. A reputation for integrity can persuade an opponent to trust you when force alone could not.
source: Livy, History of Rome 5.27; Plutarch, Life of Camillus 10
caveat: The story belongs to the early Roman tradition and is probably more moral legend than history.
